parts: You join the queue at the cinema snack counter, and then you see the price of the popcorn.
Corn, heat, a pinch of salt. How can one bucket cost this much?
Here is the surprise. At AMC, about half of your ticket money goes to the movie studio.
So the cinema needs another way to pay its bills, and it is sitting right in front of you.
Let's follow the money, starting with your ticket.
You pay for your ticket.
The cinema doesn't pay the studio a flat fee. It pays a share of the ticket sales.
In AMC's latest annual report, that share came to close to half of its ticket revenue.
And the cinema still has to pay for the building, the screens, the staff and the cleaning.
So only about half of the ticket is left for all of that.
Now walk over to the snack counter.
The studio's share is based on ticket sales, not on snack sales.
So what you spend here stays with the cinema.
And what the food and drink cost it? In AMC's report, it came to about a fifth of what it charged.
That leaves around four-fifths to pay for the staff, the rent, and the profit.
Now add it all up. Tickets plus snacks, minus the studio's share and the cost of the food and drink.
In the latest reports of AMC and Cinemark, about half or more of what is left comes from food and drink.
So that bucket is not a side business. It helps keep the lights on.
Fine, but why charge so much? Why not sell cheap popcorn and sell more?
Economists have an idea, and it starts with two kinds of moviegoers.
Some people come to splurge: big popcorn, big drink, the full experience.
Others just want the movie, and a high price makes them walk right past the counter.
The cinema can't ask which one you are, so the counter sorts you out.
The splurgers pay a lot. Everyone else pays only for the ticket. And the ticket can stay at a price that most people accept.
The combo deal works the same way. A bigger bucket, a little discount, aimed at the person who is on the fence.
And many cinemas don't let you bring your own snacks, so the counter has little competition.
To be fair, this is economists' reasoning, not a confession from the cinemas.
And here is the twist. Cinemas once didn't want popcorn at all.
A century ago, they wanted to feel like grand theaters: rugs on the floor, and no snacking.
Then the Great Depression closed cinemas by the thousands.
Just outside the doors, street vendors were already selling snacks to the crowds.
Owners got the message. Keep the ticket price low, and make your money at the stand.
One historian says popcorn really saved theaters during the Depression.
The same idea is still at work today.
So the next time you are in that queue, you know the game.
Roughly speaking, about half of your ticket pays the studio, and your popcorn pays the cinema.
Is it still a lot of money for corn? Yes. But now it makes sense.
Hard times change what people sell, and what people eat.
In the winter of eighteen seventy, a besieged city is said to have eaten its zoo. Did Paris really do it?
